title: Thermal Hall effect in elemental niobium, a two-gap superconductor
authors: Jing Zhang, Xiaokang Li, Kamran Behnia, Zengwei Zhu
abstract: Niobium holds a pivotal place in superconductivity history: it is not only the elemental superconductor with the highest critical temperature, but also a long-standing candidate for multiband pairing whose evidence has remained controversial. A two-gap scenario was proposed as early as 1959, yet experimental proof stayed elusive. Here, through thermal Hall effect measurements, we unambiguously demonstrate a crossover in transverse thermal transport below $T_{\rm c}$, where the dominant carrier switches from hole-like to electron-like upon cooling. This crossover is a clear hallmark of two distinct superconducting condensates. Fitting our data to a two-gap Bardeen-Rickayzen-Tewordt (BRT) model yields a second energy gap of approximately 0.22 $k_{\rm B}T_{\rm c}$, only 11\% of the dominant gap. This small gap size accounts for the difficulty in resolving the two-gap structure in earlier experiments. Crucially, the temperature at which the electron-like contribution to longitudinal thermal conductivity begins to dominate coincides with the onset of the sign reversal in the thermal Hall coefficient, confirming consistency between the two methods, and providing crucial information on the assignment of the superconducting gaps to their respective hole- or electron-like Fermi surface sheets. These findings not only resolve a longstanding controversy, but also establish that multigap superconductivity is far more common than previously assumed, and demonstrate the thermal Hall effect as a powerful probe for resolving gap multiplicities in superconductors.
summary: This work uses thermal Hall effect measurements on niobium to definitively prove it is a two-gap superconductor. By observing a carrier crossover and fitting the data to a two-gap model, the authors quantify a small, previously elusive second superconducting gap. This establishes the thermal Hall effect as a powerful technique for characterizing gap multiplicity in superconductors.
main_problem: To resolve the long-standing controversy regarding whether elemental niobium is a single-gap or a two-gap superconductor, and to demonstrate the thermal Hall effect as a powerful probe for resolving gap multiplicities.
main_result: The thermal Hall effect measurements unambiguously demonstrate a crossover in transverse thermal transport below T_c, confirming two distinct superconducting condensates. Fitting the data yields a small second energy gap of approximately 0.22 k_B T_c.
method: Measurements of the thermal Hall effect (kappa_xy) and longitudinal thermal conductivity (kappa_xx) are performed under applied magnetic fields, analyzed using the two-gap Bardeen-Rickayzen-Tewordt (BRT) model.
model_or_system: The study focuses on elemental niobium (Nb), a multiband superconductor. The analysis employs the two-gap BRT model to account for two distinct superconducting condensates (hole-like and electron-like carriers).
key_observables: Thermal Hall conductivity (kappa_xy), longitudinal thermal conductivity (kappa_xx), and the temperature dependence of the transverse thermal transport crossover.
important_parameters: Critical temperature (T_c), two superconducting gaps (Delta_1 and Delta_2), and magnetic field strength (up to 6 kOe).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the applicability of the two-gap BRT formalism to describe the superconducting state and that the thermal Hall effect is sensitive to the distinct quasiparticle contributions.
figures_summary: Figures show normal state transport properties, kappa_xy vs. H and T, and resolved contributions to superconducting thermal conductivity (kappa_s^h, kappa_s^e) used to extract the two gap values.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical system and the need to resolve the gap structure. It details the measurement of kappa_xy and kappa_xx, analyzes the crossover behavior, and finally fits the data to the two-gap BRT model to quantify the second gap.
why_interesting: The use of the thermal Hall effect provides a novel, robust diagnostic tool to probe superconducting gap structure, which is highly relevant for understanding complex many-body ground states in condensed matter systems.
